newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU roundtable to focus on practical aspects of EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU roundtable to focus on practical aspects of EMU.

text.p: The European Union on Thursday will hold a roundtable discussion on the practical aspects of a single currency, an effort aimed at stemming widespread confusion for consumers and businesses.

Uncertainty over how the euro will be introduced, particularly what it will mean for retailers and banks, has led the European Commission to bring together a broad array of EU officials, business executives and consumer groups.
The one-day meeting, chaired by EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy and consumer policy commissioner Emma Bonino, will focus on two specific areas.

One concerns the timetable and method by which euro banknotes and coins will be introduced, while the second will focuses on some of more personal aspects of the new currency, such the much heated issue of dual pricing.
Under the transition scenario for the euro, due to start on January 1, 1999, notes and coins will not be put into public hands until 2002 at the latest.

Until that time, national currencies will remain legal tender and in public circulation. The euro will be available in "scriptual" or electronic form, from 1999 and be used primarily by banks, corporations, governments and financial markets.

The changeover blueprint hammered out by EU finance ministers also envisages a period of double circulation, where national currencies will coexist with the euro for about six months, beginning on January 1, 2002.

Feedback to this part of the transition scenario has been controversial, with many consumer and trade associations arguing against introducing the euro on January 1. Some say the date, while psychologically important, falls during the peak retail period of Christmas and the new year.
A more quiet time frame would be preferable.
There is also a desire by some groups to shorten the six-month period of dual circulation so as to minimise the potential confusion of having to work in two currency denominations.

Other important issues are how national currencies will be converted into the euro -- rounding questions, for example -- and whether retailers will be obliged to price their goods in both national currencies and the euro.
